findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, causing cross-identity denials
findings.body: The new denial cache key is built only from the subject UID: userPermDenialCacheKey(ns, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, parent). It does not include checkReq.IdentityType nor the resolved user identifiers. Both 'anonymous:0' and 'render:0' carry UID "0", so a denied Check for an anonymous user (e.g. reading a private dashboard) stores a denial under the ..._0_... key, and the next render-service read Check for the same namespace/action/name/parent hits that entry and is incorrectly denied for up to 30s, breaking dashboard image rendering. The same key also collides when a subject is passed as a numeric user id (user:123) versus a user whose actual UID string is "123". The key must include the identity type (and should use the resolved user UID rather than the raw subject).

findings.title: Every resource absent from cached permissions now triggers a DB query
findings.body: Before this change a Check for a resource not present in the user's cached permission map was answered from the cache (deny) without touching the database. Now, whenever the cached permission map exists but does not cover the requested resource, execution falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which always queries the permission store (the in-singleflight cache read was removed). The new denial cache only suppresses repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parent) tuple, so workloads that check many distinct resources the user cannot access (a user or service account iterating/probing dashboards across an org) issue one DB query per distinct resource per 30s instead of being served from the permission cache. In large orgs this can significantly increase permission-store load.

findings.title: DB requery does not refresh the folder tree, so inherited access to new folders is still denied and cached
findings.body: The new fallback only re-queries the user's permission scopes; it does not refresh the folder tree used by checkInheritedPermissions. buildFolderTree reads folderCache (shortCacheTTL = 30s) and nothing invalidates it when a folder is created. If the tree was cached before a new child folder was created, tree.Ancestors(parent) will not include the new folder, so a user whose access to the new folder/dashboard is inherited from an ancestor is denied even though permissions were re-queried. That false denial is then written to permDenialCache, keeping the user blocked for up to another 30s after the folder tree finally refreshes. This means the PR's stated target case (newly created folders) remains broken in any busy namespace where the folder tree is already cached.

findings.title: Tests do not cover denial-cache writes or identity isolation
findings.body: The new 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test seeds permDenialCache by hand and only asserts the false result; it never exercises the code path that is supposed to populate the denial cache after a DB-backed denial, and it would still pass if the `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)` call at the end of Check were removed (the default fake store denies too). There is also no test that a denial cached for one identity type does not affect another, which is why the anonymous/"0" vs render/"0" collision above is not caught. Add a test that performs a denied Check and asserts the second call is served from the denial cache without a store call (e.g. via store.calls), and a test that a denial for anonymous:0 does not deny render:0.
